To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the tremor in normal subjects is an involuntary component of the force that is maintained in isometric conditions and that this tremor is a component of a suprasegmental system that regulates force and posture.
the tremor in Parkinson’s disease (PD) patients is characterized by a high-frequency component (8–15 Hz) and by an amplitude that increases in relation to the force applied.
the tremor is a complex phenomenon that can be divided into several components, and that these components have different frequency ranges.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the study of tremor in Parkinsonism, the characteristics of the tremor and its relation to the voluntary component of force, and the possibility of using tremor as a diagnostic and treatment criterion.
the analysis of the tremor characteristics of the hand force maintained in normal and pathological conditions.
the study of the characteristics of the oscillations in hand force in the normal state and in various pathological conditions of the central motor system.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
tremor is an abnormal movement that is not a simple oscillatory movement.
tremor is a disorder of the central nervous system and is a manifestation of the central nervous systems inability to maintain a stable posture.
the tremor is a complex phenomenon, and that the clinical diagnosis of Parkinson's disease is based on the presence of a combination of signs and symptoms, including tremor.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
tremor in the normal state and Parkinson's disease are different in terms of frequency and amplitude.
in the normal state the tremor frequency is determined by the frequency of the voluntary component.

the method of recording and analysis of the tremor of the hand muscles is a sensitive and informative method of investigation of the suprasegmental mechanisms of the control of the movement system and of the diagnosis of the central disorders of this system.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the tremor is a manifestation of the central nervous system, and it is not a disease in itself.
the tremor is a manifestation of a central disorder in the control of movement, which can be detected by the analysis of the cross-correlation function.
tremor can be recorded by tensotremorography and the frequency range of tremor in normal subjects is in the range of 4-7Hz, and in parkinsonian patients is in the range from 4-8Hz.
